Choosing a calibration

Source: vignettes/articles/choosing.Rmd
choosing.Rmd

A calibrated significance level rests on three choices: how much evidence a significant result should carry, which prior defines that evidence, and which sample size enters the calculation. All three can and should be made before the data are analyzed.

How much evidence

The target is a Bayes factor in favor of the alternative hypothesis.

Target Reading
BF = 1 The minimum: rejecting the null never means the data favor it. Rules out Lindley’s paradox.
BF = 3 Moderate evidence for the alternative.
BF = 10 Strong evidence for the alternative.

These are the conventional grades of Jeffreys, as relabeled by Lee and Wagenmakers. A target is a decision about what a claim should require; if a field or a journal sets a threshold, use it.

Which prior

The six methods fall into two families.

The four prior-fraction methods invert Jeffreys’ approximate Bayes factor, which needs only a test statistic and the sample size. They differ in b, the fraction of the data used to specify the prior. They apply to any model whose coefficient tests are Wald tests, which includes generalized linear models.

R Stata Prior fraction b When
"JAB" jab 1/n You want to be conservative against small effects.
"min" min 2/n The maximum likelihood estimate may be misspecified.
"robust" robust max(2/n, 1/√n) It may be misspecified and the sample is small.
"balanced" balanced balances the Type I and Type II errors Type II errors are costly.

The two Klauer calibrations center the alternative on an effect size you name, and answer a sharper question: which level makes a significant result evidence against an alternative centered on the effect I care about?

R Stata Prior
"ES" es A mixture concentrated around plus and minus the targeted effect de.
"moment" moment Zero density at the null value itself and little near it, so the level falls fastest with n.

Klauer, Meyer-Grant and Kellen (2025) derive these under the normal linear model. For other generalized linear models they hold in the same asymptotic sense as the prior-fraction methods; for a non-Gaussian model with a modest sample, prefer the prior-fraction methods.

If you can only name a plausible range of effects, the balanced method with a matching upper expresses that. If you can name the effect size you care about, ES or moment with de is the sharper statement. The defaults for the prior’s other parameters are those Klauer et al. recommend.

Here is what the choice does at 1,000 observations with a target of 3, and what it costs against an effect of 0.1.

Method Level for BF = 3 Power at d = 0.1
JAB 0.002550 0.55
min 0.003730 0.60
robust 0.017400 0.78
balanced 0.024200 0.82
ES 0.002190 0.54
moment 0.000491 0.37

The test and the parameters that remain

alphaN() and alphan are calibrated for the test of a regression coefficient. For the two Klauer calibrations, two further settings describe that test.

q is the number of coefficients tested jointly. The default of 1 is the t test of one coefficient; with a larger value the level applies to the F test of the joint null, and the targeted effect de is on Cohen’s f scale. Cohen (1988, chapter 9) labels f2 of .02, .15 and .35 as small, medium and large.

p is the number of parameters retained under the null, including any intercept. For the test of one coefficient, it is the number of other coefficients. The default of 0 is a conservative large-sample form; giving p produces the calibration that is exact for the normal linear model.

Which sample size

Use the number of observations in the estimation sample. With clustered or panel data the observations are not independent and that number overstates the information in the data. Wulff and Taylor (2024) recommend calibrating with the total number of observations, which is conservative, and then checking whether conclusions survive at the effective sample size:

# The cluster-robust standard error is twice the classical one
n_effective(n = 237, se = 0.1, se_robust = 0.2)
#> [1] 59.25
alphan n_effective, n(237) se(.1) se_robust(.2)

The worked example does this on a real panel.

Report what you chose

The settings report records the target, the method, its prior settings, the resulting level and the decision rule: alphaN_report() in R and alphan report in Stata. Write it down before you see the results, and attach it to the preregistration.

References

Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.

Klauer, K. C., Meyer-Grant, C. G., & Kellen, D. (2025). On Bayes factors for hypothesis tests. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 32, 1070–1094. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-024-02612-2

Wulff, J. N., & Taylor, L. (2024). How and why alpha should depend on sample size: A Bayesian-frequentist compromise for significance testing. Strategic Organization, 22(3), 550–581. https://doi.org/10.1177/14761270231214429
